title: CIPD Level 3
issuer: Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development
content_provenance: Original practice items authored from the public CIPD Level 3 Foundation Certificate syllabus (business, culture and change; people practice; core behaviours; evidence-based practice). Not a capture of past exam questions.

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: A people professional is asked to assess how external forces may affect the organisation's workforce plan over the next three years. Which framework is most appropriate for systematically reviewing the external environment?
options: PESTLE analysis, which reviews political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental factors
A training needs analysis of every team in the organisation
A review of recent grievance and disciplinary cases
An annual appraisal cycle review across all departments
items.explanation: PESTLE is the standard framework for scanning external political, economic, social, technological, legal and environmental influences on an organisation. Training, grievance and appraisal reviews are internal people processes and do not scan the external environment.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: Leaders describe the organisation as valuing open challenge and innovation, but staff say they are reprimanded for questioning decisions. What does this gap best illustrate?
options: A well-aligned and consistently reinforced organisational culture
The difference between an espoused culture and the culture that is experienced in practice
The complete absence of an organisational culture
A purely legal compliance issue with no cultural dimension
items.explanation: Espoused values are what an organisation says it believes, while the lived or experienced culture is what people actually encounter. A gap between the two is a common cultural misalignment, not a well-aligned culture, an absence of culture, or merely a legal matter.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: An organisation is restructuring and some roles will be at risk. What is the most appropriate contribution of the people function during the change?
options: Decide the new structure alone without involving any managers
Delay all communication until the change is fully complete
Advise on consultation requirements and support managers to communicate fairly and consistently
Handle the change purely as an administrative filing exercise
items.explanation: People professionals add value during change by advising on legal consultation duties and equipping managers to communicate fairly and consistently. Making unilateral decisions, withholding information, or treating change as mere paperwork all undermine trust and compliance.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: A senior team wants to understand why the organisation must change its operating model. Which approach best identifies the internal and external drivers of change?
options: Assume change is needed only because one competitor changed something
Rely solely on the personal preferences of the chief executive
Wait for a major crisis before examining any drivers at all
Analyse internal pressures such as performance and cost alongside external pressures such as market and technology trends
items.explanation: Change is driven by a combination of internal factors such as performance and cost and external factors such as markets and technology, so both must be analysed. Copying one competitor, following one person's preference, or waiting for a crisis is not a systematic identification of drivers.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: A people professional wants a structured model that describes how individuals often respond emotionally as a change unfolds over time. Which model is most relevant?
options: The Kubler-Ross change curve, which describes stages from shock and denial through to acceptance
A profit and loss forecasting model for the coming financial year
A recruitment funnel model used to track job applications
A stock valuation model used by the finance team
items.explanation: The Kubler-Ross change curve is widely used to understand the emotional stages people may move through during change, from shock and denial to acceptance. Forecasting, recruitment funnels and stock valuation are unrelated to human responses to change.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: A change programme will alter how customer service teams carry out their daily work. What should be the first step in managing the impact on those teams?
options: Issue the new procedures without any discussion or preparation
Identify the stakeholders affected and assess how the change affects each of them
Wait for complaints before engaging with the affected staff
Reassign all affected staff to other departments straight away
items.explanation: Managing the people impact of change begins with stakeholder identification and impact assessment, which then informs communication and support. Issuing procedures cold, waiting for complaints, or immediately moving staff ignores the need to understand and plan for impact.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: Research suggests that a strong, well-aligned culture can support organisational performance. Which people practice most directly helps to build and sustain such a culture?
options: Publishing values on a poster and then taking no further action
Allowing each team to define values that contradict one another
Articulating values and reinforcing them through consistent day-to-day behaviours and decisions
Changing the stated values every quarter to follow the latest trend
items.explanation: Culture is built and sustained when stated values are consistently reinforced by everyday behaviour and decisions. Posters alone, contradictory team values, or constantly changing values create confusion and weaken alignment with performance.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: A government announces new employment rights that will affect working patterns across the sector. How should the people function respond?
options: Ignore it until an employment tribunal claim arises
Apply the changes only if a competitor decides to do so
Delegate all responsibility for legal compliance to line managers
Monitor the legislation, assess its impact on policies and plan any changes needed
items.explanation: The people function should proactively monitor legal change, assess its impact on policies and practices, and plan implementation. Waiting for a tribunal, following a competitor, or pushing legal compliance onto untrained managers risks breaches and inconsistent treatment.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: The organisation plans to introduce automation that will change several roles. What is the most appropriate people practice response?
options: Assess the skills impact and plan redeployment, retraining and support for affected colleagues
Make all affected roles redundant without any assessment
Proceed without informing employees until the system goes live
Assume the affected roles will be entirely unaffected by automation
items.explanation: Technology change calls for a skills impact assessment and practical support such as redeployment and retraining. Immediate redundancy, secrecy, or assuming no impact ignores the organisation's duty to manage change responsibly and retain valuable capability.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: An organisation wants its people strategy to support its environmental and social commitments. Which action best aligns the people function with that goal?
options: Treat sustainability as an issue solely for the operations team
Embed responsible and sustainable practices into people policies and ways of working
Add sustainability wording to one policy and change nothing else
Wait for new regulation before taking any action at all
items.explanation: Aligning people strategy with environmental and social goals means embedding sustainability into people policies and everyday working practices. Leaving it to operations, adding a token sentence, or waiting for regulation fails to mobilise the workforce behind the organisation's commitments.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: Demand for a key service is expected to rise sharply next year. Which action best helps the organisation prepare its workforce?
options: Recruit only after the additional demand has already arrived
Assume existing staff will absorb all of the additional demand
Forecast the skills and headcount needed and plan recruitment and development accordingly
Freeze all recruitment to keep costs under control
items.explanation: Workforce planning uses forecasts of future demand to plan the skills and headcount required, so recruitment and development can be timed correctly. Reacting late, overloading existing staff, or freezing recruitment all create service and capability risk.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: A newly formed team is told that results matter more than relationships and that competition between members is encouraged. Which culture type does this most closely describe?
options: A collaborative and person-centred culture that prioritises wellbeing
A compliance-driven bureaucratic culture focused on rules
An informal, family-like culture focused on belonging
A results-driven, competitive culture that prioritises performance over personal relationships
items.explanation: Emphasising results over relationships and encouraging internal competition describes a results-driven, competitive culture. Collaborative, bureaucratic and family-like cultures each place different priorities on people, rules or belonging.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: Staff report rumours and heightened anxiety during a major restructure. What is the most effective action for the people function?
options: Provide clear, timely and honest communication through trusted channels
Withhold all information until every decision is final
Let the rumours settle on their own without any response
Restrict all updates to the senior leadership group only
items.explanation: Clear, timely and honest communication through trusted channels reduces uncertainty and the spread of rumour. Withholding information, ignoring rumours, or confining updates to leaders typically increases anxiety and speculation among the wider workforce.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: An organisation operates in a fast-changing market with frequent technological shifts. What does this context most require from its people strategy?
options: Rigid job descriptions that are never reviewed or updated
Flexibility and continuous learning so that people can adapt to change
A strategy based only on the assumption of long-term stability
A policy of avoiding all new technologies wherever possible
items.explanation: In a volatile environment the people strategy must build adaptability and continuous learning. Rigid job descriptions, an assumption of stability, or avoiding technology all leave the workforce unable to respond to rapid change.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.domain: Business, Culture and Change in Context
items.stem: A manager asks the people function to help reduce turnover in a team with consistently poor leadership. Which action addresses the root context most effectively?
options: Increase pay for the whole team without any diagnosis
Tell staff to be more resilient and change nothing else
Support the manager to improve their leadership behaviours while reviewing engagement and exit data
Ignore the issue because some level of turnover is normal
items.explanation: Turnover linked to poor leadership is best addressed by developing the leader and examining engagement and exit evidence together. Raising pay without diagnosis, blaming staff resilience, or accepting the problem leaves the underlying cause untouched.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Business, Culture and Change in Context

items.stem: A hiring manager wants to fill a vacancy quickly. Which approach best supports fair and effective recruitment?
options: Rely only on the interviewer's immediate gut feeling about each candidate
Shortlist only candidates who are already known to the manager
Skip the job description entirely in order to save time
Use a structured process with defined criteria and consistent assessment for all candidates
items.explanation: Structured recruitment with defined criteria and consistent assessment is fairer and more predictive than informal methods. Gut feeling, favouring known contacts, and omitting a job description all increase bias and the risk of poor or unlawful selection decisions.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: Before recruiting for a new role, what should the people professional do first?
options: Conduct a job analysis to define the duties and the knowledge, skills and behaviours required
Write the advertisement before understanding what the role involves
Set the salary before the role itself has been defined
Ask the candidates to define the role during their interviews
items.explanation: Job analysis is the foundation of recruitment because it defines the role's duties and the knowledge, skills and behaviours needed. Writing adverts, setting pay, or letting candidates define the role before analysis produces unclear and inconsistent requirements.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: A selection panel needs a method that predicts how well candidates will perform a task they would carry out in the role. Which method is most valid for this purpose?
options: A casual question about the candidate's personal hobbies
A work sample or job simulation that is relevant to the role
A decision based on the candidate's physical appearance
Asking who the candidate already knows in the organisation
items.explanation: Work samples and job simulations sample actual role behaviour and are strong predictors of on-the-job performance. Hobbies, appearance and personal connections are unrelated to ability and introduce bias rather than valid prediction.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: A recruitment panel is finalising its interview questions. What is the most appropriate way to ensure the process is fair and non-discriminatory?
options: Ask female candidates about their childcare arrangements
Ask only younger candidates about their long-term plans
Base all questions on the job requirements and apply the same criteria to every candidate
Ask different questions depending on the candidate's background
items.explanation: Fair selection asks job-related questions and applies the same criteria to all candidates. Questions about childcare, age-related plans, or different treatment based on background are discriminatory and irrelevant to the ability to do the job.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: A new starter resigns within the first month, citing confusion about their role and little support. Which action would most likely have prevented this?
options: Leaving the new starter to find their own way around the organisation
Delaying any induction until the first formal appraisal
Sending no communications at all before the start date
A structured induction covering expectations, systems, culture and a clear point of contact
items.explanation: A structured induction sets expectations and provides systems, cultural and contact information that help a new starter settle. Leaving them unsupported, delaying induction, or failing to communicate beforehand all increase early confusion and resignation risk.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: A line manager wants to help an employee who is underperforming to improve. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Hold a supportive conversation to clarify expectations and identify any barriers or support needed
Begin formal disciplinary action against the employee immediately
Move the employee to a lower grade without any discussion
Ignore the underperformance and hope that it improves on its own
items.explanation: Performance management should begin with a supportive conversation that clarifies expectations and identifies barriers and support. Immediate discipline, demotion without discussion, or ignoring the issue are premature, unfair or ineffective responses.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: A team needs clear performance objectives. Which approach best supports motivation and clarity?
options: Set deliberately impossible targets in order to stretch everyone
Set specific, measurable and achievable objectives that are agreed with the individual
Keep the objectives vague so that they cannot be challenged
Allow employees to set objectives with no link to wider team goals
items.explanation: Specific, measurable and achievable objectives agreed with the individual give clarity and support motivation. Impossible targets demotivate, vague objectives cannot be assessed, and objectives disconnected from team goals fail to align effort.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: An organisation wants its reward approach to attract, retain and motivate employees while controlling cost. Which principle best supports this aim?
options: Paying each employee a random amount to appear flexible
Ignoring external market pay data entirely when setting pay
Pay that is internally equitable and externally competitive, supported by non-financial rewards
Relying only on financial rewards and offering nothing else
items.explanation: Effective reward balances internal equity with external competitiveness and is reinforced by non-financial rewards. Random pay, ignoring market data, or relying only on money can cause unfairness, difficulty attracting talent or unsustainable cost.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: A group of employees raises a collective concern about their working conditions. What is the most appropriate response from the people function?
options: Refuse to discuss the concern with anyone at all
Threaten disciplinary action against the employees who raised the concern
Ignore the concern until it escalates into a formal dispute
Engage constructively with the employees or their representatives and follow the organisation's procedures
items.explanation: Constructive engagement with employees or their representatives, following agreed procedures, is the correct way to resolve collective concerns. Refusing to discuss, threatening discipline, or ignoring the issue damages trust and may breach legal duties.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: A new employee begins work but is not given a written statement of particulars within the required period. Why does this matter?
options: Employees are legally entitled to a written statement of key terms within the required timeframe
Written terms are entirely optional and have no legal basis at all
Only managers are entitled to receive written terms and conditions
A verbal agreement always fully replaces any legal requirement
items.explanation: UK law requires employers to give employees a written statement of key employment terms within a set period. It is not optional, it is not limited to managers, and a verbal agreement does not remove the legal duty to provide written particulars.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: A job advert specifies that candidates must be under 30 years old for a role where age is not a genuine occupational requirement. Which statement is most accurate?
options: Age limits in job adverts are always permissible in every case
This is likely unlawful age discrimination under the Equality Act 2010
Age discrimination law applies only to retirement decisions
The advert is acceptable because employers may set any criteria they wish
items.explanation: Setting an age limit that is not a genuine occupational requirement is likely direct age discrimination under the Equality Act 2010. Age limits are not always lawful and age protection is not confined to retirement, so an employer cannot simply set any criteria.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: An employer is considering dismissing an employee with more than two years' service for conduct. To reduce the risk of an unfair dismissal claim, what must the employer ensure?
options: A decision made without any investigation of the facts
Dismissal with no reason being given to the employee
A fair reason and a fair procedure, including investigation and a right to be heard
A decision taken by a single colleague with no process followed
items.explanation: Fair dismissal requires both a fair reason and a fair procedure, including a reasonable investigation and an opportunity for the employee to respond. Skipping investigation, giving no reason, or ignoring process is very likely to make a dismissal unfair.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: An organisation needs to reduce the number of employees in a particular role. What is a key legal requirement when selecting employees for redundancy?
options: Select employees based only on personal dislike
Select the newest employees automatically in every case
Avoid any consultation with the affected employees whatsoever
Use fair and objective selection criteria and consult appropriately with those affected
items.explanation: Redundancy selection must use fair and objective criteria and be accompanied by appropriate consultation. Selection on personal dislike, automatic last-in-first-out, or no consultation at all risks unfair dismissal and breaches of collective consultation duties.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: An organisation notices rising absence that is linked to stress. What is the most appropriate people practice response?
options: Identify the causes of work-related stress and take preventive action, such as reviewing workload and support
Treat all absence as a disciplinary matter without any investigation
Encourage staff to hide stress from their managers
Do nothing because stress is a purely personal issue
items.explanation: Employers have a duty to manage work-related stress, so the correct response is to find the causes and take preventive action such as reviewing workload and support. Treating stress as discipline, encouraging concealment, or ignoring it all worsen the problem.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: The people function holds personal data about employees. Which action best supports compliance with data protection law?
options: Share all employee data widely with anyone who requests it
Collect only the data needed, store it securely and retain it only as long as necessary
Keep every record indefinitely without any stated reason
Store unencrypted personal data on personal devices
items.explanation: Data protection law requires data minimisation, security and limited retention. Sharing data freely, keeping everything indefinitely, or storing unencrypted personal data on personal devices all breach the principles that protect employees' information.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Principles of People Practice

items.stem: A senior manager asks the people professional to remove a record of a complaint before an audit. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Delete the record in order to protect the senior manager
Ask a colleague to delete the record instead
Refuse and explain that falsifying records is unethical and against policy and law
Agree to delete it but keep a secret copy for later
items.explanation: Ethical practice requires refusing to falsify records and explaining clearly why the request is wrong. Deleting the record, asking someone else to do it, or secretly retaining a copy all involve dishonesty and breach policy and law.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A people professional believes a proposed restructure will damage employee wellbeing. How should they demonstrate professional courage?
options: Stay silent in order to avoid any conflict with leadership
Leak confidential information to the press instead of raising concerns
Implement the restructure without asking any questions
Raise their evidence-based concerns with decision-makers and recommend alternatives
items.explanation: Professional courage means speaking up responsibly, using evidence to raise concerns with decision-makers and proposing alternatives. Silence, leaking confidential information, or unquestioning implementation all fail the standards expected of the profession.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A colleague's contribution is consistently overlooked in team recognition. How should a people professional demonstrate that they value people?
options: Acknowledge the individual's contribution and ensure credit is given fairly
Take credit for the colleague's work in front of others
Ignore the situation because it is not their concern
Tell the colleague to submit a formal complaint about it
items.explanation: Valuing people means recognising contributions and ensuring credit is shared fairly. Taking credit, ignoring the omission, or deflecting the colleague to a formal complaint are not the inclusive, respectful behaviours the profession expects.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A team meeting is regularly dominated by the same few voices, and quieter members are not heard. What should the people professional do?
options: Allow the dominant voices to continue speaking for the group
Use inclusive facilitation to invite and value contributions from everyone
Exclude the quieter members from future meetings
Cancel the meetings altogether to avoid the problem
items.explanation: Working inclusively means facilitating so that all voices can contribute and are valued. Letting a few dominate, excluding quieter members, or cancelling the meetings reduces inclusion and loses the benefits of diverse input.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: An employee discloses a sensitive personal matter and asks for it to be kept confidential. How should the people professional handle this?
options: Share the details with the whole team immediately
Post the details on a public noticeboard in the workplace
Respect confidentiality while explaining any limits where there is a legal or safety duty to act
Promise absolute secrecy with no exceptions even where safety is at risk
items.explanation: Ethical practice respects confidentiality but is honest about the limited circumstances, such as legal or safety duties, where information may need to be shared. Broadcasting the disclosure or promising unconditional secrecy misleads the employee and can cause harm.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: The people function is asked to justify a proposed investment in training. How can it best demonstrate commercial thinking?
options: Present the proposal without any cost or benefit analysis whatsoever
Insist that the investment is made with no rationale provided
Focus only on how enjoyable the training sessions will be
Link the proposal to business outcomes and show the expected costs and benefits
items.explanation: Commercial thinking means connecting people proposals to business outcomes and setting out expected costs and benefits. Proposals without analysis, demands with no rationale, or a focus only on enjoyment do not demonstrate value to the organisation.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A people professional wants to keep their knowledge and skills current as employment law changes. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Commit to continuous professional development and reflect on learning against the profession's knowledge and behaviours
Rely only on what they learned several years ago
Avoid all further training in order to save time
Assume that the law will never change during their career
items.explanation: Continuous professional development, informed by the profession's knowledge and behaviour standards, keeps people professionals effective as law and practice change. Relying on old learning, avoiding training, or assuming no change leaves the professional out of date and exposed.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A people professional is asked for their view on a people issue. How should they use evidence to inform their response?
options: Base the response purely on personal assumption and guesswork
Draw on reliable data and credible sources and be transparent about any uncertainty
Invent statistics in order to make the case seem stronger
Refuse to engage with any evidence or sources at all
items.explanation: Insight-focused practice uses reliable data and credible sources and is honest about uncertainty. Assumption, invented statistics, or refusing to consider evidence all undermine the credibility of the people function and the quality of decisions.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A people professional has access to sensitive employee data. What is the most ethical approach to its use?
options: Share it casually with colleagues as a matter of gossip
Use it for personal advantage wherever possible
Use it only for legitimate purposes and keep it secure and confidential
Ignore all rules about confidentiality and data protection
items.explanation: Ethical use of employee data means using it only for legitimate purposes and keeping it secure and confidential. Gossiping, exploiting data for personal gain, or ignoring confidentiality rules are serious breaches of professional and legal standards.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A manager wants to reject a well-qualified candidate for a reason that appears discriminatory. What should the people professional do?
options: Accept the manager's decision without making any comment
Help the manager conceal the real reason for the rejection
Tell the candidate the true reason on the manager's behalf
Challenge the decision and advise on fair and lawful selection
items.explanation: Professional courage requires challenging a potentially discriminatory decision and advising the manager on fair, lawful selection. Accepting it silently, helping to conceal the reason, or informing the candidate improperly all fail to prevent unlawful discrimination.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A people professional notices that recruitment decisions tend to favour candidates who are similar to the existing team. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Help the panel recognise and reduce unconscious bias in their decision-making
Encourage the panel to trust their instincts even more
Ignore the pattern because it is entirely normal
Recruit only from the existing team's personal networks
items.explanation: Working inclusively means helping decision-makers recognise similarity bias and take steps to reduce it. Encouraging instinct, ignoring the pattern, or recruiting only from existing networks entrenches the bias and reduces diversity of thought.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: Two courses of action each have advantages and drawbacks, and the decision will affect several teams. What is the most appropriate approach for the people professional?
options: Choose randomly between the options in order to avoid blame
Weigh the evidence, consider the impact on stakeholders and make a reasoned, transparent decision
Avoid deciding and allow the issue to drift indefinitely
Decide purely on the basis of personal preference
items.explanation: Situational decision making means weighing evidence, considering stakeholder impact and making a reasoned, transparent choice. Random choice, endless avoidance, or personal preference do not meet the standard expected when decisions affect multiple teams.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A people professional is under pressure to present engagement survey results more positively than the data show. What should they do?
options: Alter the figures in order to please the leadership team
Omit the negative findings from the presentation entirely
Present the results accurately and explain the implications honestly
Refuse to present any data at all to anyone
items.explanation: Ethical practice requires presenting results accurately and explaining their implications honestly, even when inconvenient. Altering figures, omitting negative findings, or refusing to present data all breach the honesty expected of the profession.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: The people function wants to build trust with employees after a period of poor communication. What is the most effective behaviour?
options: Make promises that cannot realistically be kept
Communicate only when there is bad news to deliver
Ignore employee concerns until they eventually go away
Be consistent, transparent and reliable, and follow through on commitments
items.explanation: Trust is built through consistency, transparency and reliability, so commitments must be met. Broken promises, communicating only bad news, or ignoring concerns all erode the credibility the people function needs in order to influence.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: Which set of principles best reflects the professional values expected of people professionals?
options: Acting ethically, taking responsibility, being honest and treating people with respect
Prioritising personal gain above the interests of others
Avoiding accountability for decisions whenever possible
Keeping important information back to benefit oneself
items.explanation: The core professional values centre on ethical conduct, responsibility, honesty and respect for people. Personal gain over others, avoiding accountability, or withholding information for self-interest directly contradict the standards the profession upholds.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Core Behaviours for People Professionals

items.stem: A people professional wants to make decisions grounded in evidence-based practice. What does this approach involve?
options: Relying only on the opinion of the most senior person in the room
Combining the best available research evidence with organisational data and professional judgement
Using only personal intuition without collecting any data
Following whatever approach happens to be most popular on social media
items.explanation: Evidence-based practice integrates research evidence, organisational data and professional judgement rather than a single source. Seniority alone, pure intuition, or social media popularity are not reliable bases for people decisions.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: Which sources best represent the four types of evidence used in evidence-based people practice?
options: Only opinions and unverified hearsay from the workplace
Only social media posts and trending topics
Scientific research, organisational data, practitioner experience and stakeholder views
Only the personal preferences of the chief executive
items.explanation: Evidence-based people practice draws on four sources: scientific research, organisational data, practitioner experience and stakeholder views. Hearsay, social media and a single leader's preferences are not credible substitutes for these sources.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: A people professional wants to understand the reasons behind employee turnover rather than just the numbers. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Use only headcount figures with no narrative explanation
Rely on a single anonymous comment as the whole picture
Avoid asking the employees anything about their experience
Use qualitative methods such as interviews and focus groups to explore the underlying reasons
items.explanation: Qualitative methods such as interviews and focus groups are suited to exploring the reasons and experiences behind a pattern like turnover. Headcount alone, one anonymous comment, or avoiding employee input cannot explain why people are leaving.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: Data show that teams with higher training hours also have higher productivity. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: The two are correlated, but this does not prove that training caused the higher productivity
Training definitely caused the productivity increase in every single case
The data prove that there is no relationship between the two at all
The result can be ignored simply because it involves numbers
items.explanation: A relationship between two variables shows correlation, which does not by itself establish that one caused the other. Claiming definite causation, denying any relationship, or dismissing numeric evidence are all unsound interpretations.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: A people professional is choosing an assessment method for a selection process. What does validity refer to in this context?
options: The length of time that the assessment takes to complete
The extent to which the assessment measures what it is intended to measure
The colour of the assessment materials used during the session
The popularity of the assessment among the candidates being tested
items.explanation: Validity is the degree to which an assessment measures what it is supposed to measure, such as predicting job performance. Duration, appearance and popularity are not measures of validity and do not establish that an assessment is meaningful.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: The people function wants to track the effectiveness of its recruitment process. Which measure is most relevant as a key performance indicator?
options: The number of coffee cups used in the office each month
The colour of the recruitment team's stationery
Time to hire and quality of hire
The chief executive's favourite restaurant
items.explanation: Time to hire and quality of hire directly measure the speed and effectiveness of recruitment. Office consumables, stationery colours and unrelated preferences have no bearing on whether the recruitment process is performing well.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: An organisation wants to compare its absence rate with that of similar organisations. What is this practice called?
options: Guesswork with no external comparison whatsoever
Ignoring all external data and assuming internal data are best
Assuming the organisation always performs better than everyone else
Benchmarking against comparable organisations or sector data
items.explanation: Benchmarking compares an organisation's measures, such as absence rates, with those of comparable organisations or sector data. Guesswork, ignoring external data, or assuming superiority provides no meaningful point of comparison.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: Before drawing conclusions from HR data, what should the people professional check first?
options: Whether the data are accurate, complete and drawn from a reliable source
Whether the data happen to support their own preferred conclusion
Whether the data can be presented attractively regardless of accuracy
Whether the data can be shared with others without any checks
items.explanation: Sound analysis begins by confirming that data are accurate, complete and from a reliable source. Selecting data to fit a preferred conclusion, prioritising presentation over accuracy, or sharing unchecked data all undermine the credibility of the findings.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: A colleague presents a single article as proof that a new HR practice always works. How should a people professional respond critically?
options: Accept the article immediately because it has been published
Consider the quality, context and strength of the evidence before drawing any conclusion
Reject all evidence automatically without reading it
Assume that a single source is always sufficient for a decision
items.explanation: Critical thinking weighs the quality, context and strength of evidence rather than accepting or rejecting it wholesale. Accepting one article as proof, dismissing all evidence, or treating a single source as sufficient can lead to poor people decisions.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: An organisation has introduced a new wellbeing programme and wants to know whether it worked. What is the most appropriate approach?
options: Assume it worked because it was popular to launch at the time
Close the programme without carrying out any review
Evaluate the programme against pre-agreed measures and compare results over time
Ask only the programme's designer for their opinion of it
items.explanation: Evaluation requires pre-agreed measures and comparison of results over time to judge whether the programme achieved its aims. Assumption, closing without review, or relying only on the designer's opinion provides no objective evidence of impact.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: A people professional must present analysis to senior leaders who have limited time. How should the evidence be communicated most effectively?
options: Present every raw data point in full detail regardless of relevance
Use jargon that only a small group of specialists can understand
Avoid offering any conclusions or recommendations at all
Present clear, concise findings linked to business priorities, with the most important points first
items.explanation: Communicating evidence well means being clear and concise, linking findings to business priorities and leading with the most important points. Overloading detail, using impenetrable jargon, or offering no conclusions fails to influence the audience.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: A people professional wants a reliable picture of employee engagement across the whole organisation. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Use a well-designed survey with a representative sample and carefully worded questions
Ask only a single employee for their personal opinion
Base the picture entirely on informal corridor conversations
Assume engagement is good without collecting any data at all
items.explanation: A representative sample and carefully worded questions give a survey the reliability needed to represent the whole organisation. One opinion, corridor impressions, or unmeasured assumptions cannot describe engagement across a large workforce.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: A department has a sudden increase in resignations. What is the most appropriate first step in an evidence-based investigation?
options: Blame the line manager immediately without any supporting evidence
Gather and analyse exit data and other evidence to understand the underlying causes
Ignore the resignations because some turnover is normal
Announce a pay rise without understanding the actual cause
items.explanation: An evidence-based investigation starts by gathering and analysing exit data and related evidence to find the underlying causes. Immediate blame, ignoring the trend, or acting before understanding the cause risks the wrong response and repeats the problem.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: A people professional is analysing survey results and finds data that contradict their own view. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Discard the data because it disagrees with their existing opinion
Alter the data so that it matches their original opinion
Consider the evidence objectively and revise their view if the evidence supports it
Ignore the findings and proceed with the plan as originally intended
items.explanation: Working with evidence means considering it objectively and being willing to revise a view when the evidence supports it. Discarding, altering or ignoring inconvenient findings is confirmation bias and undermines the integrity of people decisions.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice

items.stem: The people function wants to use employee survey data that could identify individuals in small teams. What is the most appropriate consideration?
options: Publish individual responses with names attached to each one
Share the raw data freely with all managers across the organisation
Ignore any concerns about privacy and individual identification
Protect anonymity and confidentiality when reporting results from small groups
items.explanation: Where small groups are involved, reporting must protect anonymity and confidentiality so individuals cannot be identified. Publishing named responses, sharing raw data liberally, or disregarding privacy breaches both ethical duties and data protection law.
items.reference: CIPD Level 3 Syllabus - Evidence-based Practice
